ar_west_pinn.blurb: West Pinn, also known as Cliffbreak, is the older and more established of the two climbing sections at Rattlesnake Ridge, in the northeast part of the natural area outside Little Rock. It holds 17 routes, mostly bolted sport lines with a handful of trad and top-rope options. Grades start near 5.5 and climb past 5.12, with plenty in the 5.6 to 5.10 range, so there is something for a mixed group. The rock is sandstone. Several lines have been bolted since older topos were drawn, so route names may not match what you find.
ar_west_pinn.approach: From the parking area, follow the signs toward Cliffbreak. Service roads give the faster way in; the foot trail is a good deal longer.

ar_rock_house.blurb: Rock House is a small bouldering sector on the Mossy Bluff trail system in northeast Arkansas, set on a short, capped band of bluff just above the Flux Pavilion boulder. It has 17 problems covering the full range from very easy up to the low V8 level, with a cluster of V0 to V4 lines and a few hard ones at the top end. The sandstone is firm, with better quality than the boulders below it, and many problems top out. After a problem, most climbers walk back down the Mossy Bluff trail to the base.

ct_porcupine_wall_climbs.blurb: Porcupine Wall is a short crag on Rattlesnake Mountain in Connecticut's Central Valley, with a handful of good lines among its 17 routes. The climbing is mostly traditional with some top-rope, and grades run from easy 5th class through the 5.8 and 5.9 range, topping out at a single 5.11. The wall sits in shade most of the day, which makes it a pleasant choice in summer. Of the Rattlesnake Mountain walls, it is the first one you reach on the ridge trail, and the trail's start can be muddy.
ct_porcupine_wall_climbs.approach: Leave the car at the pull-off on Route 6, take the short access path to the blue-blazed Metacomet Trail, and head south. This is the first of the crags along the trail.

ct_green_wall.blurb: Green Wall is a shady crag a short way north of the main Rattlesnake Mountain cliff in Connecticut's Central Valley. It holds 17 routes, all on gear or top rope, ranging from scrambly easy terrain through the 5.4 and 5.5 range up to a good group at 5.9. Several carry protection warnings, so check route notes before committing to a lead. The Metacomet Trail runs near the top of the wall, and the cool, shaded face suits warm days.
ct_green_wall.approach: Reach it from the Metacomet Trail, walking south from the Route 6 parking area; it is the second crag along that path, after Porcupine Wall.

ct_upper_ledges.blurb: The Upper Ledges are a big friction slab at St. John's Ledges in Kent, Connecticut, rising well over 100 feet in places and likely the second tallest slab in the state. Of the 17 routes here, most are top-rope, with a few trad lines and a scramble. Grades concentrate in the 5.7 to 5.9 range with a couple at 5.10. The slab splits into the longer Super Slab, which is loose and open, and the Trail Magic section on the left, where leading is more realistic. Protection is sparse, there are no bolts, and the crag draws many school and camp groups.
ct_upper_ledges.parking_note: Park along River Road, at the point where the Appalachian Trail crosses it.
ct_upper_ledges.approach: Walk uphill on the Appalachian Trail from River Road; the trail runs along the foot of the slab, so watch where you place gear.

ct_broken_bridge.blurb: Broken Bridge is a small bouldering area in Killingworth, Connecticut, in the pockets of rock around Chatfield Hollow State Park. It has 17 problems, mostly from V1 through V5 with a few harder ones reaching V7 and V8. The gneiss faces west beside a small swamp. Quality ranges from excellent to flaky, and moss is common, so a stiff nylon brush helps. You cross a small stream at the broken bridge and the boulders are just beyond.
